sections.skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection

questions.prompt: Ana misses a credit card payment by 10 days. Which consequence is MOST likely first?

choices.text: A fee for paying late
Immediate arrest
Her wages are garnished the next day
A 30-day late mark on her credit report

questions.intro: Consequences of a missed payment build over time. Right after the due date, the issuer can charge a late fee. Once a payment is 30 or more days past due, it can be reported to credit bureaus. Debts left unpaid for months can go to collectors or court.
questions.feedback: At 10 days late, a late fee is the likely consequence; credit reporting generally starts at 30+ days late.
questions.topic: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy

misconceptions.D: A payment is not reported late until it is 30 or more days past due

questions.prompt: A 30-day late payment was reported in March 2020. Under the usual rule for negative items, about when should it drop off Ana's credit report?

choices.text: Around March 2021
Around March 2030
Around March 2027
Never; late payments stay forever

questions.intro: Under federal law, most negative items stay on credit reports for 7 years. Some bankruptcies can stay for up to 10 years. Positive information can stay longer.

questions.prompt: A debt collector calls about an old debt Sam does not recognize. What right does he have?

choices.text: To have the whole debt erased simply by asking for that
To make the collector pay him for the call
None; collectors can say anything
To dispute the debt and receive validation information

questions.correct_answer: To dispute the debt and receive validation information
questions.intro: The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act gives consumers rights: collectors must provide validation information about the debt, consumers can dispute it, and collectors may not harass, threaten, or lie.
questions.feedback: He can dispute the debt; the collector must provide information validating it.

questions.prompt: A collector threatens to have Rina arrested over a $400 credit card debt. What is true?

choices.text: This threat is illegal; debt is not a crime
She must pay immediately or go to jail
Collectors may say anything to get paid
Arrest is a normal step for unpaid debts over $300

questions.correct_answer: This threat is illegal; debt is not a crime
questions.intro: Collectors may not threaten arrest or legal action they cannot or do not intend to take.
questions.feedback: Threatening arrest for ordinary debt is a prohibited practice. She can report it to the CFPB.

questions.prompt: What is bankruptcy?

choices.text: A free way to cancel all debts with no consequences
A payment plan arranged by a debt collector
A court process to erase or reorganize debts
A credit score below 500

questions.correct_answer: A court process to erase or reorganize debts
questions.intro: Bankruptcy is a federal court process. Chapter 7 can discharge many debts, sometimes after selling some assets; Chapter 13 sets a repayment plan, usually over 3–5 years. Some debts, such as most student loans and child support, are hard or impossible to discharge.
questions.feedback: Bankruptcy is a serious legal option of last resort with lasting credit effects.

misconceptions.B: Confuses bankruptcy with a repayment plan
misconceptions.D: Confuses a legal process with a credit rating

sections.skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
sections.relationship: Students must know what a due date and late fee are before reasoning about collections and credit damage.

questions.prompt: A bill says "Due June 15." Ali pays on June 18. What usually happens?

choices.text: He may be charged a late fee
Nothing, because three days is close enough
The bill is cancelled
He earns interest

questions.correct_answer: He may be charged a late fee
questions.intro: A due date is the deadline for a payment. Paying after it can bring a late fee and, if very late, other consequences.
questions.feedback: Paying after the due date can trigger a late fee.

questions.prompt: A card's minimum payment is $35 on a $900 balance. If Ali pays $35, what happens to the rest?

choices.text: It is forgiven
It is paid by the card company
It must be paid separately in cash at a bank branch
It carries over and can be charged interest

questions.correct_answer: It carries over and can be charged interest
questions.intro: The minimum payment is the smallest amount that keeps an account in good standing that month. It does not pay off the balance.
questions.feedback: The remaining $865 carries over, often with interest.

questions.feedback: Autopay for at least the minimum, plus extra when possible, prevents late payments.

questions.prompt: Sam wants a collector to stop calling. Under federal rules, what can he do?

choices.text: Nothing; calls cannot be stopped
Pay a fee to stop the calls
Ask his bank to block the debt from being collected
Ask in writing that it stop contacting him

questions.correct_answer: Ask in writing that it stop contacting him
questions.intro: Consumers can tell a debt collector in writing to stop contacting them. The collector may then contact them only to confirm or to say it will take a specific action, such as filing a lawsuit. The debt itself still exists.
questions.feedback: A written request stops most contact, though the debt remains and the collector may still sue.

questions.prompt: Sam receives a debt validation notice on May 1 and believes the amount is wrong. By about when should he send a written dispute so the collector must verify the debt before continuing?

choices.text: By about May 31
By May 4
By about November 1
Any time, since there is no deadline

questions.intro: After a collector first contacts you, it must send validation information. If you dispute the debt in writing within the validation period (generally 30 days), the collector must pause collection until it verifies the debt.
questions.feedback: About 30 days from May 1 is May 31.

questions.prompt: Which collector behavior is prohibited?

choices.text: Calling repeatedly to harass
Sending a letter with the amount owed
Calling during normal hours to ask for payment
Offering a payment plan

questions.intro: Collectors may contact you to collect, but federal law bans harassment, threats, false statements, and unfair practices.
questions.feedback: Harassment, such as repeated calls meant to annoy, is prohibited.

The CFPB or the state attorney general

questions.prompt: A collector offers to settle a $2,000 debt for $1,200. What should Sam get before paying?

choices.text: Nothing; a phone promise is enough
A promise over the phone only
A new credit card from the collector
The settlement agreement in writing

questions.intro: A settlement is an agreement to pay less than the full balance. Get the terms in writing before paying, and keep proof of payment.
questions.feedback: A written agreement protects against later claims for the rest.

7 years
10 years
0 years

questions.intro: Most negative items stay on a credit report for 7 years from when the trouble began.
questions.feedback: 7 − 3 = 4 more years (generally measured from the original delinquency).

questions.prompt: Which action usually helps a credit report recover over time?

choices.text: Opening many new cards at once
Ignoring all mail from creditors
Paying a company to erase accurate negatives
Making every new payment on time

questions.correct_answer: Making every new payment on time
questions.intro: The impact of old negative items fades over time, especially when new on-time payments build a better record.
questions.feedback: Recent on-time payments gradually outweigh older problems.

questions.prompt: A company promises to remove ACCURATE negative information from a credit report for $500. What should a consumer know?

choices.text: Paying more guarantees removal
It is the only way to fix credit
Accurate negatives cannot be removed early
The credit bureaus require consumers to buy this service

questions.correct_answer: Accurate negatives cannot be removed early
questions.intro: You can dispute inaccurate information for free. Accurate negative information generally stays for the time allowed by law, no matter who you pay.
questions.feedback: Credit repair cannot remove accurate information; disputing errors is free.

questions.prompt: In some states, making a small payment on a very old debt can do what?

choices.text: Erase the debt entirely
Guarantee a perfect credit score
Make the debt illegal to collect from that point on
Restart the time limit for a lawsuit on that debt

questions.correct_answer: Restart the time limit for a lawsuit on that debt
questions.intro: A statute of limitations limits how long a creditor can sue over a debt. It varies by state, and in some states a payment can restart the clock.
questions.feedback: Before paying an old debt, learn your state's rules on the statute of limitations.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Chapter 13 bankruptcy is TRUE?

choices.text: It erases every debt instantly
It is the same as a debt management plan from a counselor
It sets a court-approved repayment plan, often 3–5 years
It has no effect on credit

questions.correct_answer: It sets a court-approved repayment plan, often 3–5 years
questions.intro: Chapter 13 bankruptcy reorganizes debts: a person with regular income repays creditors through a court-approved plan.
questions.feedback: Chapter 13 reorganizes debts into a repayment plan, usually 3–5 years.
